title: A compositional calculus for concurrent systems that fail

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a practical method for calculating system guarantees from the contracts of its components, even when those components run concurrently, share memory, exchange messages, and experience partial failures. A component contract would describe what the component guarantees and what it requires from its surroundings. Mechanically checked composition rules would determine whether connected components jointly provide specified safety, crash-recovery, and progress guarantees. The distinctive target is to make this combined capability usable by ordinary systems engineers maintaining production services. This is the proposed scope, rather than an established achievement.

The method would connect contracts to executable implementations through component verification. Given those verified contracts, the connection structure, and explicit execution and failure assumptions, engineers could derive system properties without repeatedly inspecting every implementation detail. Replacing a component with another implementation verified against the same contract would preserve the applicable system derivation. Existing work already demonstrates parts of this approach: DeepSpec describes compositional verified layers, CertiKOS demonstrates interchangeable implementations in a concurrent kernel, and Yggdrasil provides modular crash refinement and substitution for single-threaded storage systems.

significance.text: The potentially revolutionary step is usable integration across concurrency, communication, and partial failure. Within a soundly modeled scope, incompatible component assumptions and guarantees would become mechanically checkable obligations, and verified replacement could preserve system guarantees without reconstructing the whole argument. This would extend benefits already demonstrated in narrower settings: CertiKOS supports substitution between lock implementations with the same interface, while Yggdrasil allows higher layers to reason from lower-layer specifications and permits replacement by implementations satisfying the same crash specification.

As an explanatory analogy, structural engineering reasons about an assembly through the properties of its parts and their connections. The proposed software calculus would offer a comparable discipline for specified behavioral guarantees. The analogy concerns reusable reasoning; it does not imply that software behavior is already captured by simple numerical formulas. As a conditional downstream possibility, stable contracts and reusable proofs could make service upgrades, component procurement, and architectural experimentation easier to assess. These are enabling possibilities, not evidence of adoption or measured economic impact.

The guarantees would remain conditional on adequate specifications, implementation conformance, sound composition rules, and valid environmental assumptions. A hidden implementation defect cannot be discovered from an unchanged contract alone. Failures excluded by the proved properties would be ruled out within the model; arbitrary distributed failures would not all become composition-time errors. DeepSpec explicitly conditions its anticipated benefits on suitable externally visible specifications and modeling assumptions. Performance envelopes and physical timing remain outside this candidate's proposed scope.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target is a mechanically checked composition method that jointly handles shared memory, message passing, partial failure, executable implementations, component substitution, and practical maintenance. Existing results mean that composition and substitution themselves cannot be treated as missing inventions. The unresolved integration question is whether these capabilities can be combined across the stated service scope with routine engineering usability. DeepSpec documents historical gaps between verified components and the research needed to connect them, but the supplied evidence does not establish that the full target remains unavailable as of November 1, 2026.

A central scientific barrier is aligning what each layer promises with what the surrounding layers actually assume. DeepSpec's two-sided specification goal addresses this connection between clients and implementations. For the proposed calculus, contracts must expose enough information about concurrency, communication, failure, and recovery to support valid system conclusions. They must also hide enough implementation detail to permit useful substitution. A proof about a design model does not by itself establish that executable code follows that model, as the retained account of Amazon's 2015 TLA+ experience makes explicit.

Engineering synthesis: the combined method would need compatible semantics for shared state, messages, crashes, and recovery; explicit rules for discharging each component's assumptions; and progress arguments that state scheduler and communication conditions. It would also need tooling that keeps contracts and implementation proofs aligned as software changes. These are concrete obligations implied by the proposed scope, rather than a claim that every existing framework lacks them.

Usability is a separate barrier from logical soundness. DeepSpec identifies an education gap between verification researchers and practitioners. A production-ready method would need comprehensible contracts, actionable explanations when composition fails, and maintenance costs that engineers can sustain through releases. The supplied Iris abstract establishes an implemented verification foundation, but does not establish either that it is expert-only or that it already meets this broader usability target.

current_state.text: DeepSpec's undated research overview describes significant specification gaps in its network of verified components, says that closing them generally requires research breakthroughs, and identifies additional work needed on concurrency and distributed programming in its Clight specification. These statements document the programme's integration challenges; they do not establish that the same gaps remain unchanged in 2026. The supplied review relied on the overview's prose and did not inspect its associated diagram.

The 2017 position paper, The science of deep specification, defines deep specifications as rich, two-sided, formal, and live, connecting precise behavioral descriptions with the needs of clients and proved implementations. It presents broader end-to-end integration and practitioner adoption as a research programme while also reporting existing compositional successes, including certified layers in CertiKOS. It therefore supports both the integration ambition and the existence of substantial prior capabilities.

The separate 2016 CertiKOS paper supplies direct evidence of compositional reasoning in a concurrent kernel. The passages identified in the review discuss deriving global properties through the kernel specification and treating ticket-lock and MCS-lock implementations as interchangeable because they share an interface. The retained PDF extraction has missing-text warnings, and its figures were not inspected; these limitations restrict claims about the whole document, while leaving the reviewed passages available as evidence for these narrower results.

The separate 2016 paper Push-Button Verification of File Systems via Crash Refinement describes Yggdrasil's automated, modular reasoning about crash-safe storage. Programmers supply a behavioral specification, an implementation, and consistency invariants. Higher layers can use lower-layer specifications without reasoning about implementation details, and implementations satisfying the same specification can be substituted. Its stated single-threaded scope is a material boundary: this result demonstrates important crash-reasoning and substitution capabilities without completing the candidate's combined concurrency and distributed-service target.

The retained source for Iris from the ground up is the abstract and bibliographic landing page for the 2018 Journal of Functional Programming paper, volume 28, article e20. It establishes that Iris is a framework for higher-order concurrent separation logic, implemented in Coq and used across a variety of verification projects. The supplied review did not have the full 73-page paper in this retained source. The abstract supports the existence and deployment of the framework, but cannot settle its present industrial accessibility or justify classifying it as usable only by experts.

The Amazon evidence is Lamport's highly abridged account of the April 2015 Communications of the ACM paper, with omissions and editorial additions relative to the original. It reports successful industrial use of TLA+ for design verification alongside an unproved connection between the verified designs and executable code. This is evidence of the benefits and limitations reported at that time, not a statement of Amazon's verification capabilities in November 2026.

NSF's Software and Hardware Foundations synopsis includes compositionality and verifiability among its research topics. This establishes research-programme scope, rather than either the existence or absence of an industrial calculus meeting this candidate's requirements.

Evidence synthesis: the supplied material establishes substantial dated foundations and historical integration challenges. No bounded contemporary search record was supplied, so it does not determine whether a production-ready method meeting the complete target was available on November 1, 2026. That freshness limitation does not invalidate the documented results or establish that the proposed combined capability has been achieved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: rebuild a production service from components with explicit contracts and mechanically checked evidence that their implementations satisfy those contracts. Publish the composition topology, shared-memory and message semantics, crash and recovery model, and relevant environmental assumptions. From the verified contracts, connection structure, and assumptions, a tool should derive specified system safety and crash guarantees plus at least one meaningful liveness property under explicit scheduler and communication conditions. This is a proposed evaluation, not an established benchmark.
completion_criteria.label: Production service safety, crash, and liveness derived from checked contracts

completion_criteria.text: Proposed substitution and rejection tests: replace a component with another implementation verified against the same contract and retain the system derivation without changing its reasoning about that component. Introduce an incompatible contract and show that composition rejects it. Separately inject an implementation violation and show that component verification rejects the implementation or its claimed certificate. An unchanged contract cannot itself reveal a hidden defect in the code behind it.
completion_criteria.label: Same contract substitution retains derivation and rejects mismatches

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and usability tests: make the contracts, implementations, proofs, checker versions, assumptions, and build instructions available for independent reproduction. Have engineers who are not proof specialists maintain the derivation through a production release, recording the assistance required and the effort needed when components change. Exercise representative concurrent interactions and failure-recovery scenarios to clarify the relationship between the formal model and the running system; such exercises complement the proof rather than replacing it.
completion_criteria.label: Non-specialists maintain a reproducible derivation through a production release

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: report precisely which properties, components, failure modes, and environmental conditions the demonstration covers, together with trusted tools and dependencies. A successful service and release would establish feasibility within that scope. Additional independently reproduced systems would broaden the evidence, but finite demonstrations would not establish literal universality. Performance envelopes and physical timing need not be included to satisfy this candidate's stated target.
completion_criteria.label: Report the demonstration's precise scope, trusted tools, and dependencies

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison with SWE-01, Push-button verifying compilation for practical systems, and SWE-02, Certified synthesis of system-scale programs from reviewable specifications: these concern obtaining verified executable systems through compilation or synthesis. SWE-04 concerns deriving guarantees for connected components and preserving them through verified substitution. Compilation or synthesis could provide component-conformance evidence, but even a complete monolithic proof does not automatically provide reusable composition and substitution rules.

Roster-based comparison with SWE-03, Demonstrable adequacy of a specification against intent and the environment, and SWE-06, Sound behavioral recovery of legacy systems: specification adequacy concerns whether the formal statement captures what is wanted and what the environment permits; behavioral recovery concerns obtaining trustworthy descriptions of existing systems. Either could supply essential inputs to SWE-04. A sound composition proof remains conditional on those inputs and does not independently establish that contracts capture human intent or faithfully describe unverified legacy code.

Roster-based comparison with SWE-05, Assurance that stays proportional to each behavioral change, and SWE-11, Proved semantics-preserving transformation of practical systems: reusable component proofs could reduce the assurance work associated with a change, linking SWE-04 to SWE-05. Substitution under an unchanged contract is nevertheless narrower than a general method for keeping assurance proportional to arbitrary behavioral changes. SWE-11 concerns preservation through program transformations; SWE-04 concerns guarantees across connected components, including replacements that may differ internally while satisfying the same contract.

Roster-based comparison with SWE-07, Practical confinement of general untrusted programs, and SWE-10, Proof-carrying behavioral composition across trust boundaries: confinement could make an environmental or isolation assumption enforceable, while proof-carrying composition could communicate and check evidence between parties. SWE-04's focus is the composition calculus spanning concurrency and partial failure. Trust-boundary evidence delivery is a related concern, but the supplied title does not justify reducing SWE-10 to third-party checking of shipped binaries.

Roster-based comparison with SWE-08, Sequential meaning for fault-tolerant distributed execution, and SWE-09, Observable determinism as the default for parallel systems code: both could simplify the behaviors that a composition method must consider. SWE-08 emphasizes the relationship between distributed fault-tolerant execution and sequential meaning; SWE-09 emphasizes observable behavior under parallelism. SWE-04 does not require every component to have sequential semantics or deterministic observations, but would need contracts and rules that account soundly for whichever behaviors its components permit.

These comparisons preserve the roster entries as distinct innovations. Only their titles and the candidate's brief boundary statements were supplied, so the relationships are conceptual interpretations rather than validated comparisons of full specifications.

unresolved_issues: Whether a production-ready method meeting the full combined target existed as of November 1, 2026 remains unresolved because no bounded contemporary search record was supplied.
The supplied evidence does not quantify the effort, training, or maintenance cost required for ordinary systems engineers to use the existing foundations or the proposed integrated method.
The candidate does not yet specify its exact shared-memory, messaging, crash-recovery, scheduler, and communication models or its trusted computing base.

brief.title: Software guarantees that survive changes and failures
possible: Engineers could replace part of an online service without rebuilding the argument that the whole service behaves correctly. Each part would have a contract stating what it promises and what it needs. Tools would combine contracts checked against running code, even when parts share memory, exchange messages and fail separately.
why: Teams maintaining services could check whether components’ promises and assumptions fit together. Reusable proofs could make upgrades and changes to system design easier to assess, without repeatedly examining every component’s internal details.

sources.showed: Its research programme includes combining guarantees about software parts and checking software correctness.
sources.cited_for: The programme treats reasoning about systems through their parts as a research topic.
sources.not_established: A funding programme does not demonstrate a working method for production services.

sources.who: Chris Newcombe and colleagues at Amazon Web Services
sources.showed: Amazon engineers used TLA+, a language for precise system models, to find design bugs. Their account did not prove that executable code followed those models.
sources.quote:
In several
cases, we have prevented subtle but serious bugs from reaching
production.
sources.cited_for: Checking precise designs can find bugs that ordinary engineering checks miss.
sources.not_established: A checked design does not establish that the executable implementation obeys it.

sources.showed: The team found that independently verified components could rely on incompatible descriptions of the same programming language.
sources.quote: What we often find in practice (for example) is that the C language spec used in proving CertiKOS does not match the C language spec delivered by CompCert.
sources.cited_for: Component contracts must match what surrounding components actually require.
sources.not_established: The overview does not demonstrate an integrated method covering concurrent services and partial failures.

sources.showed: The authors described contracts tied to both code and its users. They reported experiments connecting checked correctness proofs across teams.
sources.quote: We identify an important class of specification that has already been used in a few experiments that connect strong component-correctness theorems across the work of different teams.
sources.cited_for: Checked proofs about separate components can already be connected in narrower settings.
sources.not_established: These experiments do not establish routine maintenance of the full proposed service scope by ordinary engineers.

sources.showed: Iris provides mathematical rules for checking programs whose parts run at once. It is implemented in Coq, a tool that checks proofs, and has served multiple verification projects.
sources.quote: Iris is a framework for higher-order concurrent separation logic, which has been implemented in the Coq proof assistant and deployed very effectively in a wide variety of verification projects.
sources.cited_for: Implemented tools already support proofs about interacting parts that run at once.
sources.not_established: This result does not establish the combined failure-handling method or its usability for ordinary service engineers.

shown: CertiKOS demonstrated reasoning from component guarantees in a kernel, the core of an operating system, including interchangeable implementations. Yggdrasil demonstrated reusable crash-recovery proofs and replacement of storage components, but only when execution follows a single sequence rather than concurrent activity.
missing: A combined demonstration must cover shared memory, messages, partial failures and recovery, with contracts proved against executable code.
System proofs must survive compatible replacements, while checks reject incompatible contracts and code that violates its contract.
Engineers without proof expertise must demonstrate that they can maintain the guarantees through a production release.

milestones.label: A service’s safety, recovery and progress follow from contracts
milestones.explanation: Checked component contracts would have to establish a production service’s safety, crash recovery and continued progress under stated conditions. This would demonstrate the combined capability.

milestones.label: Compatible replacements preserve proofs and mismatches are rejected
milestones.explanation: A replacement meeting the same contract would have to preserve the system proof; checks would reject incompatible contracts and implementation violations. This would establish reusable reasoning through component changes.

milestones.label: Ordinary engineers maintain independently reproducible proofs through a release
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce the proof, and engineers without proof expertise maintain it through a production release with recorded effort. Failure exercises would help connect the model to running behaviour.

milestones.label: The demonstration’s coverage and trusted dependencies are explicit
milestones.explanation: The demonstration would have to state its covered properties, components, failures, conditions and trusted tools. This would define where its guarantees apply without claiming that a finite demonstration covers every system.

uncertain: Whether a production-ready method already meets the full combined target remains unresolved.
The training, assistance and maintenance effort ordinary engineers would need remain unquantified.
The exact rules for memory, messages, recovery and scheduling, and which tools must be trusted, remain unspecified.

page.title: Compositional verification of concurrent crash-recovering services
page.definition: Machine-checked rules derive a service's safety and progress guarantees from component contracts: formal statements of assumptions and guarantees. The rules cover shared-memory threads, messages and independent crashes with recovery, and engineers without formal-methods expertise can preserve the proof through a compatible component replacement.

goal.need: Grove's 2023 extended manuscript reports the source and verification artifacts tabulated below for one distributed-systems library. Its client proofs use component specifications, allowing implementation changes without reconstructing every client argument. These counts illustrate the amount of verification material whose reuse matters; line counts do not establish labour costs.

figures.caption: Verification artifacts for Grove's component library, 2023
figures.note: Figure 17 totals. Trusted network and filesystem wrappers are excluded from the verified implementation count.

statements.quote: Therefore, we envision this network of verified software components, connected by deep specifications—specifications that are rich, live, formal, and two-sided.
statements.context: Here, 'live' means connected mechanically to implementation code; 'two-sided' means exercised by implementations and clients.

statements.quote: A goal of the PROVERS program is to enable traditional software developers to incrementally produce and maintain high-assurance national security systems.
statements.context: FAQ answer 23 concerns usability and maintenance; it does not prescribe the combined concurrency and failure model of this entry.

statements.body: US National Science Foundation, Software and Hardware Foundations programme
statements.quote: SHF supports research projects focusing on program analysis and synthesis, compositionality, verifiability and adaptability of software
statements.context: Programme scope includes compositional verification; this passage sets no acceptance threshold.

completion.title: Non-experts preserve a service's compositional safety and progress proof through component replacement.
completion.criterion: For one executable service using shared-memory threads and network messages, developers without formal-methods expertise replace a component with another implementation verified against the same contract and successfully recheck the system proof. Machine-checked composition rules derive safety, crash-recovery correctness and eventual completion of specified client operations from verified contracts, including independent node crashes and recovery under stated scheduler, communication and failure assumptions. Unchanged client proofs remain valid. The trusted tools and execution model delimit the guarantee.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback combining DeepSpec's integration goal with PROVERS' non-expert maintenance goal.
completion.basis: Searches of NSF SHF, DeepSpec, DARPA PROVERS and the CertiKOS, Perennial, Grove and Welder papers found no acceptance test joining shared memory, messages, crash recovery, liveness, substitution and non-expert maintenance. This fallback uses one service and one compatible replacement, without assigning an unsupported effort, training or adoption threshold.

milestones.title: Concurrent components refine their contracts under every permitted client and thread interleaving.
milestones.criterion: Machine-check contextual refinement: a component implementation composed with any permitted client has only behaviours allowed by its specification, under the stated environment assumptions. This permits composition through specification interfaces. CertiKOS reported the result for its mC2 kernel, comprising 6,500 lines of C and x86 assembly, in 2016; its ticket-lock and MCS-lock implementations share an interchangeable interface.
milestones.set_by: Contextual-refinement convention, instantiated by the CertiKOS developers in OSDI 2016, abstract and §2.
milestones.threshold_quote: the implementation of each such function will behave like its specification under any kernel/user context with any valid interleaving.

milestones.title: A concurrent storage implementation refines its specification across crashes and recovery.
milestones.criterion: Machine-check concurrent recovery refinement: every code execution corresponds to specification transitions with identical external I/O. A crash followed by recovery, including further crashes during recovery, simulates one atomic specification crash. Perennial demonstrated this for Mailboat's mailbox library in 2019. The SMTP/POP3 implementation was unverified; the prototype proved safety and did not support composing abstraction layers.
milestones.set_by: Refinement convention, extended to concurrent recovery refinement by the Perennial developers, SOSP 2019, §3.1 and theorem 2.
milestones.threshold_quote: every sequence of code transitions must correspond to some interleaving of spec transitions with the same external I/O

milestones.title: A distributed key-value store remains linearizable through concurrent operations and node recovery.
milestones.criterion: Prove replica crash-idempotence, safe reconfiguration with valid replicas, correct client initialization and linearizable Put/Get/CondPut operations by composing component specifications. Linearizable operations appear atomic and respect real-time ordering. Grove's 2023 vKV development meets these four obligations with threads, unreliable messages and independent node crashes; it does not prove liveness.
milestones.set_by: Linearizability and crash-safety conventions, instantiated by Grove's published top-level specifications, §5.1.
milestones.threshold_quote: A clerk’s Put(k,v), Get(k), and CondPut(k,e,v) functions behave as though accessing a local in-memory key-value map with linearizable operations.

milestones.title: Compatible controller contracts compose to prove eventual stable reconciliation of a cluster.
milestones.criterion: Under Welder's weak-fairness, eventual fault-cessation and Pod-naming assumptions, prove CORE: compatible controllers eventually reach and maintain their desired states when those desired states stabilize, while respecting non-interference guarantees. Discharge their liveness dependencies and verify Rust implementation conformance to the models. Welder reported this for four composed controllers in 2026: ReplicaSet, Deployment, StatefulSet and RabbitMQ. The model uses API-server-mediated state; direct shared-memory threads lie outside its scope.
milestones.set_by: Machine-checked specification-satisfaction convention; Welder developers' controller-specific CORE criterion and composition rules, SOSP 2026, §§3–5.
milestones.threshold_quote: CORE states that a set of controllers 𝑆 collectively reconcile the cluster state to eventually match the desired state stably.

milestones.title: One service composes safety, recovery and progress proofs that survive a compatible replacement.
milestones.criterion: One executable service has checked implementation-conformance proofs and sound composition rules covering shared-memory threads, network messages, independent node crashes and recovery together. Its component contracts derive system safety, recovery correctness and eventual completion of specified client operations under explicit environmental assumptions. Replacing a component with another implementation verified against the same contract preserves the client derivation. This establishes the technical integration before the non-expert maintenance test.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback: searches of DeepSpec, PROVERS and the cited correctness papers found no published gate for this combined technical integration.

not_found: No published demonstration was found of non-experts maintaining a service proof that covers the complete technical scope.
The supplied deep-specification article's PMC full text and attempted publisher and repository copies could not be retrieved.

results.finding: Iris 3.1 provides a Coq-implemented framework for concurrent separation logic; no component sample size is stated.
results.detail: The reported framework bears on machine-checked reasoning about concurrency, but the supplied text does not report contextual refinement of a component under arbitrary permitted clients.
results.quote: Iris is a framework for higher-order concurrent separation logic, which has been implemented in the Coq proof assistant and deployed very effectively in a wide variety of verification projects.

results.finding: CertiKOS machine-checked contextual refinement for the mC2 concurrent kernel, comprising 6,500 lines of C and x86 assembly.
results.detail: The proof applies to permitted clients in the modeled x86 subset and assumes sequential consistency for atomic instructions. The machine does not model TLBs, and the assembler, bootloader, pre-initialization module and ELF loader were not verified.
results.quote:
All our proofs (including every step in Fig. 5 and Fig. 2)
are implemented, composed, and machine-checked in
Coq.

results.finding: CCAL machine-checks contextual refinement for 6 verified concurrent components, including ticket and MCS locks.
results.detail: The model assumes strong sequential consistency for shared primitives; its multithreaded model does not allow preemption. The supplied text identifies a conference paper but does not state its peer-review status.
results.quote:
To evaluate the framework itself, we have
implemented, specified, and verified various concurrent pro-
grams in the framework.

results.finding: Mailboat: 1 concurrent mailbox library verified for crash recovery using Perennial in 2019.
results.detail: The proof covers safety under Goose’s process-crash model. The SMTP/POP3 protocol implementation was unverified, and Perennial did not support composing abstraction layers. The source identifies conference proceedings but does not state whether the paper was peer reviewed.
results.quote:
The proof is machine-checked and, if correct, implies that
all possible code executions are allowed by the specification.

results.finding: DaisyNFS: 1 concurrent file-system implementation has a stated crash-safe refinement theorem.
results.detail: The theorem covers matching network I/O traces across crashes and restarts. The supplied text does not explicitly establish that crashes during recovery simulate one atomic specification crash. The proof also relies on trusted assumptions connecting Dafny and Coq, and the network dispatch loop is unverified.
results.quote:
Execution might involve crashing and restarting a program
(potentially multiple times), wiping out any in-memory state
after each crash.

results.finding: Grove verifies one distributed key-value store, vKV, using composable component proofs.
results.detail: The text describes linearizability, reconfiguration, unreliable messages and independent crashes, including during recovery. It does not explicitly establish replica crash-idempotence or prove correct client initialization. Grove does not verify liveness.
results.quote:
Nevertheless,
these proofs still compose into a complete proof of the entire
distributed system.

results.finding: Welder verified CORE for a composition of 4 Kubernetes controllers.
results.detail: The paper reports composition and resolved liveness dependencies, but the provided text does not explicitly establish Rust implementation conformance to the models. It also assumes Retry-on-Conflict loop termination to address version-conflict starvation.
results.quote:
We verified that the composition of the four controllers
implements CORE.
